item.title: If you're not frustrated you're not learning:
item.description:
If you're not frustrated you're not learning:

Errors are what generate plasticity. The reaches and failures signal to the nervous system that this isn't working, so the circuitry starts to shift.

The brain doesn't understand frustration as an emotional state. It understands the neurochemicals errors release: epinephrine and acetylcholine, then dopamine once you start approximating the right behavior.

The few people who can stay in that feeling do exceedingly well. The ones who can't generally don't learn much.

Errors plus corrective feedback drive learning; frustration itself isn't required, and heavy frustration can hurt performance.

@hubermanlab

items.title: Adderall. What does it actually do for those without clinical level ADHD? Paul Conti MD explains.
items.description: Adderall. What does it actually do for those without clinical level ADHD? Paul Conti MD explains.

item.title: What studying on Adderall does to your brain:
item.description:
What studying on Adderall does to your brain:

- Short term you're more alert and can study longer. That part is real
- What comes with it: impaired judgment, higher anxiety, more impulsive decisions, and a more suspicious defensive view of the world
- Psychosis is rare, but young people using Adderall or Ritalin to study have ended up in the hospital screaming that someone is trying to hurt them
- You don't notice any of it. Your brain changed and you still call it "just using it to study"

On non-prescribed use: studies show little real cognitive gain without ADHD. Don't stop prescribed ADHD medication without your doctor.

Dr. Paul Conti on @hubermanlab

item.title: Stop asking what you want to achieve:
item.description:
Stop asking what you want to achieve:

Ask who you wish to become. Then ask how your habits are casting votes for that person.

Study 20 minutes on Tuesday night and you cast a vote for being studious. Shoot a basketball for an hour and you cast a vote for being a basketball player.

Do that for three or six months and you cross a threshold where it becomes part of your story. Then you fight to keep the habit. You go for a run because you're a runner, not because you have a half marathon in three months.

How long a habit takes to stick varies widely - weeks to a year - and the habit - identity link is mostly correlational.

@JamesClear on @hubermanlab

item.title: Fastest way to calm down in real time:
item.description:
Fastest way to calm down in real time:

- Big inhale through your nose, maximizing the inflation of your lungs
- Before you exhale, sneak in a second brief inhale through the nose, even a tiny one
- That second inhale reopens whatever aveole collapsed in your lungs
- Then a long extended exhale through the mouth
- One is usually enough to drop your stress. Sometimes it takes two or three
- Discovered by physiologists in the 1930s and hardwired into your nervous system

Research tested ~5 min of daily cyclic sighing; a single sigh may help, but guaranteed one-breath relief isn't proven for everyone.

@hubermanlab

item.title: 14 yoga teachers claimed they can switch nostrils at will:
item.description:
14 yoga teachers claimed they can switch nostrils at will:

All 14 enlisted saying they could shift nasal airflow from left to right by thought alone, no finger plugging.

Zero succeeded.

One sat there saying "I'm switching now" while the recording showed no change at all.

Based on unpublished lab data from 14 practitioners - a small sample, not peer-reviewed proof that this is impossible.

Dr. Noam Sobel on @hubermanlab
